tasks.short: Read the safety announcement, demonstrate oxygen masks, seat belts and life jackets, and brief exit-row and special-needs passengers.

steps.what: Flight attendant announces safety and emergency procedures over the public address system
Flight attendant demonstrates oxygen masks, seat belts and life jackets
Flight attendant briefs exit-row passengers and passengers with special needs

tasks.design: On aircraft with cabin screens, a recorded announcement in the needed languages plays with the safety video, so the attendant does not read it over the PA. Demonstrating equipment (attendants stand in the aisles during the video) and briefing exit-row and special-needs passengers stay with the attendant.
tasks.previous_blocker: Announcements were read aloud on every flight, sometimes in several languages.
tasks.enabler_now: Cabin systems play recorded safety announcements and videos.
tasks.still_hard: Older aircraft without screens need the full live demonstration.
tasks.human_edge: Noticing a passenger who did not understand the briefing.

reach.learn: Whether recorded announcements free time before departure.

evidence.claim: Cabin systems on aircraft with screens can play recorded safety announcements and videos.
Aviation rules require passengers to be briefed on safety before take-off.

assumptions: Boundary: from boarding complete to special briefings done; take-off is outside.
Input contract: recorded announcements approved by the operator's cabin safety department; fallback is reading aloud.
Demonstrating and special briefings keep their full time. About a fifth of flights are on aircraft with cabin screens, where the attendant only starts the recording, so s1 keeps 80.
unknowns: Share of aircraft with cabin screens.
research_questions: Do passengers pay more attention to recorded or live briefings?

incremental.description: Flight attendant checks the recording played in full.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: only about one flight in ten has cabin screens, so s1 keeps 90 (3.5); high: a fifth of flights have screens as assumed (7.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Watch passengers during boarding and flight, read the list of special passengers, inform the purser and captain of threats, write the incident report and submit it.

steps.what: Flight attendant monitors passenger behavior to identify threats to the safety of crew and passengers
Flight attendant reads the printed list of special passengers
Flight attendant informs the purser and captain of threats
Flight attendant writes the incident report after the flight: on a paper form today; on the tablet after the change, with flight, date and seat filled in
Flight attendant checks the final incident report: what happened is described as seen, and flight, seat and people named are right
Flight attendant sends the checked incident report to the safety department: handed over on paper today; sent from the tablet after the change

tasks.design: The crew tablet ({OPS_SYSTEM}) shows the special passenger list from departure control with seat numbers, instead of a printed sheet. The incident form on the tablet fills flight, date and seat from the flight data, and the attendant writes what happened, checks the report and sends it to the safety department. Watching passengers and informing the purser and captain stay with the attendant; no camera or software watches passengers.
tasks.previous_blocker: Lists were printed and incident reports written on paper after landing.
tasks.enabler_now: Crew tablets receive passenger lists and host incident forms.
tasks.still_hard: Threats show in behaviour no list can predict.
tasks.human_edge: Calming a tense passenger before anyone else notices.

reach.learn: Whether tablet reports arrive the same day.

evidence.claim: Crew tablets can receive passenger lists from departure control and host incident forms.
Air carriers fall under NIS2 Annex I, so crew devices fall within the carrier's security duties.

assumptions: Boundary: from passengers on board to the submitted report; follow-up by the safety department is outside.
Input contract: special passenger list from departure control; flight data from the operations system; fallback is printed lists and paper forms.

Watching, informing and the check keep their full time. s4 keeps 80 because only flight, date and seat fill in and the attendant writes what happened; s5 keeps 25 for the send; s2 keeps 70 because the list comes on the tablet instead of being collected on paper.
Passenger data on the tablet are deleted after the flight.
research_questions: Do reports reach the safety department sooner?

incremental.description: Flight attendant syncs the tablet after landing.

approvals.approved_version: The incident report exactly as checked by the attendant in s4c, sent once from the tablet to the safety department for this flight; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: tablets are often offline, so about half of the reports stay on paper (s4 keeps 90, s5 keeps 60) (5.5); high: reports are written and sent on the tablet (6.9).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Walk the aisles to check seat belts, seat backs, bags and electronics, check overhead bins are closed, and report the cabin secure.

steps.what: Flight attendant walks aisles to verify that passengers have complied with regulations before take-off and landing
Flight attendant checks that overhead bins are closed and confirms the zone is secure before reporting
Flight attendant reports the zone secure to the purser: by interphone today; by the zone's cabin-ready signal where the panel has it

tasks.design: On aircraft whose attendant panel has a cabin-ready signal, each attendant presses it for their zone instead of calling the purser on the interphone, and the purser sees all zones at once. Walking the aisles and checking bins stay with the attendant.
tasks.previous_blocker: Each zone reported by interphone call to the purser.
tasks.enabler_now: Some attendant panels send a cabin-ready signal per zone.
tasks.still_hard: Older aircraft have no such signal.
tasks.human_edge: Spotting the bag wedged under a seat that a quick glance misses.

reach.task: Report cabin ready to the cockpit
reach.learn: Whether zone signals shorten the ready report.

evidence.claim: Some cabin attendant panels can send a cabin-ready signal per zone.

assumptions: Boundary: from the cabin before take-off to the cabin-secure report; the cockpit's checklist is outside.
Input contract: zone signals where the aircraft has them; fallback is the interphone.
Walking the aisles and checking bins keep their full time. About two thirds of the fleet have a cabin-ready signal, which takes a fraction of an interphone call, so s3 keeps 50.
research_questions: Does the ready report reach the cockpit sooner?

incremental.description: Flight attendant resets a wrongly pressed signal.

approvals.approved_version: The cabin-secure report for the attendant's own zone, given once after the checks in s1 and s2, to the purser by the zone signal or interphone; if anything changes in the zone the report is withdrawn and given again.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: only about a third of the fleet has the signal, so s3 keeps 75 (2.0); high: two thirds of the fleet have it as assumed (4.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Make the landing announcement, collect rubbish and stow the galley, prepare passengers and cabin for landing, signal the cockpit, and log cabin defects.

steps.what: Flight attendant makes the landing announcement
Flight attendant collects rubbish and stows galley equipment
Flight attendant prepares passengers and aircraft cabin for landing following procedures
Flight attendant confirms the cabin is ready: passengers seated and belted, galley stowed, bins closed
Flight attendant signals the cockpit that the cabin is ready: by interphone today; by the cabin-ready signal where the panel has it
Flight attendant writes cabin defects in the cabin log: on paper today; on the tablet after the change, with aircraft and flight filled in
Flight attendant checks the final defect entries: each defect is described as found, with the right seat or item
Flight attendant sends the checked defect entries to maintenance: hands over the paper log at the gate today; sends them from the tablet after the change

tasks.design: On screen-equipped aircraft a recorded landing announcement plays. Where the panel has it, the attendant confirms the cabin is ready and gives the cabin-ready signal instead of an interphone call. Cabin defects are written on the crew tablet in an electronic cabin log with aircraft and flight filled in; the attendant checks the entries and sends them to maintenance, instead of handing over the paper log at the gate. Stowing, preparing passengers and the cabin stay with the attendant.
tasks.previous_blocker: Announcements were read live and defects written in a paper log handed over at the gate.
tasks.enabler_now: Electronic logbooks with input masks sync defects to maintenance.
tasks.still_hard: Short turnarounds leave little time to enter defects before landing.
tasks.human_edge: Getting a frightened passenger into the brace-ready position calmly.

reach.learn: Whether earlier defect entries shorten turnarounds.

evidence.claim: AVIATAR Technical Logbook offers prefilled text, input masks, offline sync and a link to the maintenance system.
Three months after an electronic technical logbook rollout on 140+ aircraft, calls to maintenance control fell by more than 25%.

assumptions: Boundary: from the start of descent to defects with maintenance; disembarkation is outside.
Input contract: defect types set by cabin maintenance; recorded announcements approved by cabin safety; fallback is the paper log and live announcement.

Stowing, preparing and both checks keep their full time. s1 keeps 80 because about a fifth of flights have screens; s4 keeps 50 because two thirds of the fleet have the signal; s5 keeps 85 because only aircraft and flight fill in and the attendant writes each defect; s6 keeps 25 for the send.
research_questions: Are defects fixed on the next turnaround more often?

incremental.description: Flight attendant syncs the tablet if it was offline.

approvals.approved_version: The cabin defect entries exactly as checked by the attendant in s5c, sent once from the tablet to maintenance for this aircraft; any change needs a new check.
The cabin-ready signal for this landing, given once to the cockpit after the confirmation in s4c; if anything changes in the cabin the signal is withdrawn and given again.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: older aircraft dominate, with few screens and signals (s1 keeps 90, s4 keeps 75), and short turnarounds leave defects on paper about half the time (s5 keeps 95, s6 keeps 60) (2.9); high: the fleet mix as assumed (6.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The flight attendant keeps safety demonstrations, watching passengers and preparing the cabin; reading announcements, interphone reports and paper logs shrink.
skills_to_grow: Logging defects on the crew tablet
role.ambitious_version: An attendant with more time for passengers who need help.
